lessons.title: Reading a Term Sheet: Economic Terms vs Control Terms

children.text: A term sheet arrives as four or five pages, mostly non-binding, written in language that sounds procedural. Founders read the valuation, feel relief, and skim the rest. The rest is where the deal actually is. Every clause in a term sheet answers one of two questions: who gets the money, and who gets to decide. Sort them into those two buckets and the document stops being intimidating.

body.text: Valuation decides how the upside is split. Liquidation preference decides what happens if the upside never arrives, and control terms decide who runs the company in between. Two out of three of those are usually negotiated badly, because founders spend all their leverage on the first.

children.text: The Two Buckets

body.caption: What every term sheet clause is really about

cells: Valuation, option pool, liquidation preference, anti-dilution, dividends, pro-rata rights
Who gets how much money, and in what order
Board composition, reserved matters, information rights, founder vesting and lock-in
Who decides what, and what you can no longer do alone
Drag-along, tag-along, right of first refusal, exit obligations
Who can sell, when, and who they can drag along with them
Exclusivity or no-shop, confidentiality, conditions precedent, expenses
How the deal gets from signed term sheet to money in the bank

body.label: Most of a term sheet is not binding
body.context: Valuation, preference and board seats are commercial intent, not contract. Confidentiality, exclusivity or no-shop, and who pays the legal costs usually are binding. Exclusivity is the one to watch: sign a 60-day no-shop and you cannot talk to other investors for 60 days, however slowly diligence goes.

children.text: Liquidation Preference: The Term That Decides Bad Outcomes

markDefs.definition: The investor chooses either the preference amount or their percentage share of the proceeds, whichever is higher. They cannot take both.
The investor takes the preference amount first and then also shares the remaining proceeds by percentage. They take both.

children.text: A liquidation preference says who gets paid first when the company is sold. The market standard in India is 1x
non-participating
, which means the investor gets their money back or their percentage, whichever is larger. The aggressive version is
participating
, sometimes called double dipping, where they take their money back and then share what is left.
An investor puts ₹20 crore into an illustrative company for 25%. Here is what the founders and other shareholders receive at two different exits, under three different preference structures.

body.caption: Exit proceeds split three ways (₹20 crore invested for 25%)

body.text: Read the ₹60 crore column. Under a 2x participating preference, a company sold for three times what the investor put in leaves the founders and employees with ₹15 crore out of ₹60 crore, despite owning 75% on paper. Preference terms matter most exactly when the outcome is mediocre, which is the most likely outcome for any startup.

body.title: Run the waterfall
body.prompt: An investor holds a 1x participating preference on ₹20 crore invested for 25% of a company. The company sells for ₹100 crore. How much does the investor receive, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: The investor first takes back ₹20 crore, leaving ₹80 crore. They then also share that remainder by percentage: 25% × ₹80 crore = ₹20 crore. Total ₹40 crore. Under a 1x non-participating preference they would have taken the higher of ₹20 crore or 25% of ₹100 crore, which is ₹25 crore. The word participating cost the other shareholders ₹15 crore.

children.text: Anti-Dilution: Protection If the Next Round Is Cheaper

If a later round is priced below what this investor paid, anti-dilution improves their conversion ratio so they end up with more equity shares. Two versions exist, and the gap between them is enormous.

body.caption: Broad-based weighted average: A is shares outstanding before the new round, B is the new money divided by the old price, C is the new shares actually issued

body.title: Worked example: full ratchet vs weighted average

children.text: An investor put ₹5 crore into CCPS at ₹100 per share, so 5,00,000 preference shares. The company has 10,00,000 shares outstanding. A year later it raises ₹2 crore in a down round at ₹50 per share, issuing 4,00,000 new shares.
Full ratchet:

the conversion price simply resets to the new price of ₹50. The investor's ₹5 crore now converts into 10,00,000 equity shares instead of 5,00,000. Their position doubles, entirely at the expense of the founders.
Broad-based weighted average:

Same down round, same investor. Full ratchet gives them 10,00,000 shares, weighted average gives 5,83,333. The difference of over 4 lakh shares comes straight out of founder and employee ownership. Broad-based weighted average is the market standard in India, and full ratchet should be pushed back on hard.
Control: Board Seats and Reserved Matters

markDefs.definition: A list of decisions the company cannot take without the investor's written consent, regardless of how small their shareholding is.

children.text: Owning 20% does not usually give an investor control of a vote.
Reserved matters

do something more targeted: they give a veto over specific decisions. A typical Series A list covers issuing new shares, changing the Articles, borrowing above a threshold, selling the company, related-party transactions, the annual budget, senior hires, changes to the ESOP pool and winding up.

stats.label: Typical seed board
stats.context: Founders retain the majority of seats

stats.label: Typical Series A board
stats.context: The independent seat often becomes the swing vote

stats.label: Observer seat
stats.context: A common compromise for smaller investors

body.text: Watch the thresholds inside reserved matters. "Investor consent for any expenditure above ₹5 lakh" sounds like governance and functions as a leash on daily operations. Push for thresholds that scale with the company, a defined response time so silence does not block you, and consent that lapses if the investor's shareholding falls below a floor.

body.title: The same clause, founder-friendly and aggressive

columns.label: Market standard in India
points: Founders keep a majority of board seats at seed
Reserved matters limited to genuinely major decisions
Founder vesting over four years with credit for time already served
Drag-along that triggers only above an agreed price

columns.label: Terms to push back on
points: Participating preference, or any multiple above 1x
Consent needed for routine spending or hiring
Founder vesting restarted from zero with no credit
Drag-along at any price, forcing a sale founders oppose

body.title: Economics or control?
body.question: Which of these clauses is a control term rather than an economic one?
options: A requirement that the investor consents before the company borrows more than ₹1 crore
Pro-rata rights allowing the investor to maintain their percentage in future rounds
body.explanation: A consent requirement for borrowing is a veto over a decision, which is control. Preference, anti-dilution and pro-rata rights all decide how money and ownership are distributed, which is economics. Founders often concede control terms cheaply because they do not read them as costing anything.

children.text: Transfer and Exit Clauses

body.caption: Who can sell, and who comes along

cells: The company or investors can match any offer before you sell shares to an outsider
A time limit, so a sale is not blocked indefinitely
If founders sell, investors can sell the same proportion on the same terms
If enough shareholders approve a sale, everyone must sell
A minimum price, a minimum return, and a time gate before it can be used
Founders must help deliver an exit by a stated date, sometimes through a buyback or sale
Longer horizons, and no personal financial obligation on founders
Founders cannot leave or start something similar for a period
Scope limited to the actual business, and a sensible duration

body.title: Three things to fight for
body.scenario: Priya has a Series A term sheet for ₹25 crore at ₹100 crore pre-money. The key terms: 1x participating liquidation preference, full ratchet anti-dilution, a 5-member board with 2 investor seats and 1 independent nominated by the investor, investor consent required for any hire above ₹25 lakh salary and any spend above ₹10 lakh, founder vesting restarted over 4 years with no credit for the 3 years already worked, a 75-day no-shop, and drag-along exercisable at any price after year 3.
body.prompt: She has limited negotiating capital. Which three terms should she prioritise, and what should she ask for?
body.modelAnswer:
Rank by how much damage each does in the most likely outcomes.
1. Liquidation preference. Ask for 1x non-participating, which is the Indian market standard. On a ₹200 crore exit, participating costs the other shareholders roughly ₹15 crore, and the damage is proportionally worse in a mediocre exit, which is the likeliest case. This is the single highest-value change.
2. Anti-dilution. Ask for broad-based weighted average instead of full ratchet. Full ratchet punishes founders brutally for one bad round, and often makes a rescue round impossible because nobody wants to fund a company where a prior investor's stake balloons.
3. Board and the independent director. Two investor seats plus an investor-nominated independent means founders can be outvoted on a 5-member board at Series A. Ask that the independent be appointed by mutual agreement, which is standard, or reduce to one investor seat.
Also worth cheap asks, since they usually get conceded: credit for the 3 years already served in the vesting schedule, spending and hiring thresholds raised to sensible operating levels with a consent deadline, a no-shop cut to 45 days, and a minimum price on the drag-along.
What she should not do: spend all her leverage arguing the ₹100 crore up to ₹115 crore. The preference and anti-dilution terms are worth far more than ₹15 crore of headline valuation in almost every scenario that actually happens.

body.title: Term sheet red flags
steps: Any liquidation preference above 1x, or any participating preference.
Full ratchet anti-dilution instead of broad-based weighted average.
Investor control of the board at seed or Series A, including an investor-appointed independent.
Reserved matters covering routine operations, with no consent deadline or shareholding floor.
Founder vesting restarted with no credit for time already served.
An exclusivity period longer than 45 to 60 days, or with no expiry.
Drag-along with no minimum price or time gate.
Guaranteed returns, redemption rights or anything that behaves like debt dressed as equity.
Legal costs of the investor charged to the company with no cap.

body.title: The binding bit
body.textWithBlank: Most of a term sheet is non-binding, but the ___ or exclusivity clause is binding and stops you from talking to other investors for a set period.
body.explanation: Signing a no-shop ends your competitive process, which is your main source of leverage. Keep it short, ideally 45 to 60 days, and make sure it lapses if the investor delays.

cards.definition: The right to be paid first on a sale, usually at least the amount invested.
The investor takes either the preference amount or their percentage, whichever is higher, not both.
The investor takes the preference amount and then also shares the remaining proceeds by percentage.
Anti-dilution that resets the conversion price to the new lower price, maximally favouring the investor.
Anti-dilution that adjusts the conversion price partially, based on how much cheap stock was issued. The Indian market standard.
Decisions the company cannot take without investor consent, regardless of shareholding.
A clause forcing all shareholders to sell if a defined majority approves a sale.
A binding exclusivity period during which the company cannot negotiate with other investors.

points: Sort every clause into economics, control, transfer or process, and the term sheet stops being intimidating.
Most of a term sheet is non-binding, but confidentiality, expenses and the no-shop usually are. Keep exclusivity short.
Liquidation preference decides mediocre outcomes. A 2x participating preference can leave 75% owners with a quarter of a ₹60 crore exit.
Ask for 1x non-participating. It is the Indian market standard and worth more than several crore of headline valuation.
Anti-dilution should be broad-based weighted average, never full ratchet, which can double an investor's position after one down round.
Reserved matters are a veto, not a vote. Watch for thresholds that turn governance into operational control.
Spend your negotiating capital on preference, anti-dilution and board composition before arguing about valuation.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, investment or financial advice. Term sheet conventions vary by investor, stage and market conditions, and the clauses described here are simplified for teaching. Always have a term sheet reviewed by a qualified lawyer before signing. Priya's company and all figures are illustrative.
